title: Integrating MQL5 with Data Processing Packages (Part 11): Multi-Timeframe Causality Detection using Granger Analysis
text:
Table of Contents
Introduction
System Overview
Getting Started
Environment and Configuration
Load the Historical Data
Feature Engineering
Label Generation
Granger F-Test
Evaluation and Visualization
Results and Export
Exploratory Calibration
Putting it all Together on MQL5
Where the Live Test Differs from the Notebook
Backtest
Conclusion
Introduction
Most multi-timeframe setups rest on an assumption nobody checks: that the higher timeframe tells the lower timeframe something useful. We put an H1 trend filter on an M15 entry, or require M30 and M5 to agree, and move on. Whether the H1 bars actually carry information about the next M15 bar, beyond what the M15 bars already know about themselves, is rarely tested. If that relationship is weak, the extra timeframe is just another condition that cuts trades without improving them. If it is strong only some of the time, a fixed rule will be right in one regime and quietly wrong in the next.
Granger causality is a direct way to test this. The idea is simple: if the past values of series X improve the forecast of series Y beyond what Y's own past already provides, then X "Granger-causes" Y. It says nothing about real-world cause and effect, only about predictive content, and that is exactly the question a trader should ask about a higher timeframe. We run this test in Python, where the statistics tools are mature and easy to cross-check, then carry the result into MQL5 where a simplified version of the same test is recomputed on live data and used as a gate for signals.
The part that makes this interesting is that the result is not guaranteed to be flattering. On EURUSD, under the criterion we set before looking at the output, all four pairs came back INVALID. One pair, M30 -> M15, was promoted to VALID only after we relaxed the stability threshold, which means its status is exploratory rather than a clean pass. Two independent checks in the notebook, a heteroskedasticity-robust test and an out-of-sample comparison, do not support it either. We are keeping the pair in the system so the machinery can be shown end to end, and we say plainly throughout the rest of the article what that costs us in terms of interpretation. Fo
r the same reason, the backtest at the end is presented as a demonstration that the pieces work together, not as evidence that the filter improves trading.
System Overview
We split the work into two stages that share one contract: the same alignment rule, and the same lag structure. The first stage runs in Jupyter Lab. We pull OHLC for M5, M15, M30 and H1 from the terminal through the MetaTrader 5 Python package, convert closes to log returns in basis points, and build a design matrix for each pair. For a pair like M30 -> M15, every row is one closed M15 bar. The target is that bar's return. The regressors are the last q M15 returns and the last p completed M30 bar returns. We fit two OLS models, one with only the M15 lags (restricted) and one with the M30 lags added (unrestricted), and compare them with an F-test. Lags are chosen by BIC, significance is corrected across the four pairs with Benjamini–Hochberg, and we check how often the relationship holds on rolling 1,500-bar windows. That rolling share is what we call stability. A pair is VALID when its adjusted p-value is below alpha and its stability clears a threshold. The notebook writes all of this to 'granger_mtf_causality.csv' in the terminal's Common\Files folder.
The second stage is the EA. It reads the CSV on startup, so it knows which pairs to track, which lags to use, and what the offline verdict was. It then repeats the Granger test itself on the most recent 1,500 bars of each pair, every few bars, using a small OLS solver written in MQL5 and the F-distribution from the standard library. The fitted unrestricted model gives a forecast of the current lower-timeframe bar return, and that forecast becomes a vote. The final signal comes from counting votes, but only from pairs whose status is VALID when the filter is on. The EA draws a panel with the status of each pair, can show or hide the signals, publishes the filter state as terminal global variables for other EAs, and can trade the signals with ATR-based stops.
The live test is a simplified version of the offline one, not an exact copy. The MQL5 solver adds a small ridge term, it compares a raw p-value against alpha with no multiple-testing correction, it has no robust-covariance variant, and it looks at one window instead of measuring stability across many. A dedicated section below lists every one of these differences, because "the same test in both places" would be an overstatement.
There is one caveat worth stating up front, because it changes how the whole study should be read. On a single symbol, the higher-time
frame series is not independent. It is constructed from lower-timeframe bars
. An M30 log return is the sum of the two M15 log returns inside it, and an H1 return is the sum of four. So the "lead" regressor is a mechanical aggregate of lower-timeframe history, and a significant F-statistic has at least two possible readings. It can mean that longer-horizon structure carries information the short own lags miss. It can also mean the restricted mod
el uses too few own lags. In that case, the higher-timeframe aggregate merely substitutes for omitted M15 lags
. Our design cannot separate those two explanations. A fair test of "does an external driver push this market around" needs two different instruments, not two timeframes of one.
Getting Started
Environment and Configuration
The notebook needs MetaTrader 5, pandas, numpy, scipy, statsmodels and matplotlib, all installable with a single pip cell. The terminal must be open and logged in before running. The configuration cell at the top is where the experiment is defined:

'PAIRS' lists the relationships to test, always written as (lead, lag) where the lead is the higher timeframe. WINDOW is shared with the EA: whatever window the notebook uses for its rolling stability scan, the EA uses the same number when re-running the test live. STABILITY_MIN is the threshold that ultimately decided whether M30 -> M15 would be VALID on EURUSD; we will come back to that when the results arrive.
Two val
ues in that cell need a warning label. STABILITY_MIN = 0.60 is the criterion we fixed before running anything, and it produces the main result of this study. A second, exploratory run with STABILITY_MIN = 0.35 supplies the calibration file the EA and the backtest reads; it is described separately under Exploratory Calibration, because that threshold was chosen after seeing the first result. REQUIRE_OOS_EDGE is left at False, which means a pair can be marked VALID even when its out-of-sample behavior is worse than the baseline model. A confirmation run would set it to True; the protocol is given at the end of the backtest section.
CALIB_END pi
ns the last day of calibration data, so the CSV can be built strictly before a backtest starts. Left at None, the window ends at the current date.
'DATA_SOURCE' can be set to "csv" on subsequent runs once the data has been saved, which lets you iterate on the analysis without reconnecting to the terminal every time.

Our first attempt used copy_rates_from_pos with a bar count sized for a full year. M15, M30 and H1 came back fine, but M5 failed with (-2, 'Terminal: Invalid params') because the requested count exceeded MetaTrаder 5's internal limit. Switching to copy_rates_range with a date window fixed it, and reducing the history to 150 days kept the bar counts manageable. 150 days of M5 is still roughly 25,000 bars, far more than the 1,500-bar rolling window needs.
The iloc[:-1] on the last line matters more than it looks. The most recent bar is still forming, so its close will change. Letting it into the dataset would give the test a small peek at the future on the boundary row. We drop it here so that every row in the returned frame is a confirmed closed bar.

Any violation raises immediately rather than producing a silent bug later in the F-test.
One scheduling detail decides whether this whole study is honest or not. Every table in this article was produced with CALIB_END = None. The last closed bar in the downloaded data was on 21 September 2026, so with DAYS_OF_HISTORY = 150 the calibration window runs from about 24 April to 21 September 2026. The backtest later in the article runs from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2024, which lies entirely before that window, so the calibration file the EA reads shares no bars with the period it trades. Setting CALIB_END to a date before the first backtest bar achieves the same separation when the test period comes later. The order is unusual, though: the calibration comes from a later period than the test. The backtest therefore asks whether the 2026 verdict carries over to earlier data. It is not a simulation of live use, because nobody trading in 2023 could have known that verdict.

The alignment step is the most important part of the whole pipeline, and it is where multi-timeframe work usually goes wrong. For each lower-timeframe bar that opens at time t, we are only allowed to use higher-timeframe bars that had already closed by t. A higher bar closes at its open time plus its period, so the rule is: use higher bars whose open time is at or before t - lead_period.
'searchsorted' with side="right" minus one gives the index of the last higher bar whose open time is at or before the cutoff. From there, xlag1 is the most recent completed higher bar, xlag2 the one before it, and so on.
One design decision here is worth explaining. A more obvious approach would be to forward-fill the higher-timeframe return onto every lower bar and then take ordinary lags of that filled series. The problem is that consecutive lags of a forward-filled series are mostly identical values: four consecutive M15 bars all share the same H1 return, so the lag columns become nearly collinear. Lagging in units of completed higher bars avoids that duplication and is easier to interpret: "do the last p closed M30 bars help predict the next M15 bar?"
It reduces the problem, it does not remove it. Because the higher bar is an aggregate of lower bars on the same symbol, xlag1 and the own lags still overlap mechanically. For M30 -> M15 with q=2, on every row where the M15 bar opens at the top of an M30 bar, xlag1 is exactly ylag1 + ylag2. On the rows where it opens mid-M30, the overlap is partial. So the design matrix contains a column that is, on a repeating subset of rows, a linear combination of columns already in the restricted model. The matrix is not singular, and the regression runs, but the F-test is not cleanly measuring "new information from a higher timeframe" the way it would with two separate instruments.
Label Generation
The target variable y is already defined in build_design: it is the log return of the current lag-timeframe bar in basis points. There is no separate label generation step here the way there would be in a classification pipeline. The Granger test is a regression problem, and the label is the raw return we are trying to forecast. What matters is the sign of the forecast, which becomes the vote direction, and the magnitude relative to the return standard deviation, which is controlled by InpMinEdgeSigma in the EA.
Lags are selected by BIC over a grid of p from 1 to 4 and q from 1 to 6, fitted on the first 70% of each pair's data. On EURUSD, BIC picked p=1 for every pair, with q=2 for M30 -> M15 and q=1 for the others. That is a small model, which is what we would expect when the effect, if any, is modest.
Selecti
ng lags and testing the selected model on the same data inflates significance
. The p-value that comes out of granger_test assumes the model was fixed in advance. Ours was not: it won a search over 24 combinations. Nothing in the pipeline corrects for that search, so the reported p-values are optimistic, and the true error rate of the whole procedure is higher than the alpha we compare against. The clean alternatives are to pick p and q on a separate slice of data and never touch them again, or to fix them by argument rather than by search. We mention this here rather than burying it, because it also affects the rolling stability figures that use the same selected lags.
Granger F-Test
The test is the comparison of two nested OLS models:
def
granger_test(D, p, q):
    Xr, Xu, y = design_matrices(D, p, q)
    beta_u, rss_u = ols(Xu, y)
    beta_r, rss_r = ols(Xr, y)
    n, k = Xu.shape
    df2 = n - k
    F =
max
(((rss_r - rss_u) / p) / (rss_u / df2),
0.0
)
return
{
"F"
: F,
"p_value"
:
float
(stats.f.sf(F, p, df2)),
"df2"
: df2,
"beta_u"
: beta_u,
"beta_r"
: beta_r,
"sigma_y"
:
float
(np.std(y))}
The Xr holds a constant plus q own lags. Xu adds the p higher-timeframe lags. If the extra columns reduce the residual sum of squares by more than chance would allow, F is large and the p-value is small.
We wrote this by hand rather than calling grangercausalitytests from statsmodels, because that function assumes both series share the same lag structure and sampling frequency, which is not our case. To verify the implementation, the evaluation cell refits the same models using
sm.OLS(...).compare_f_test(...) and asserts that the p-values match. It also runs an HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test on the higher-timeframe coefficients, because intraday returns are not homoskedastic and the classical F-test can overstate significance when they are not. That check is not decoration. For M30 -> M15 the classical p-value is 0.0019 and the HC3 p-value is 0.1100, and the second number is the one to believe when residual variance clusters the way intraday returns do. We still report the classical p-value as the headline figure because it is what feeds the VALID rule and what the EA re-computes, but a pair whose significance evaporates under a robust covariance estimator has not really been shown to be significant.
The rolling stability scan repeats the test on every consecutive window of WINDOW bars, stepping forward by STEP each time:

The stability figure is the fraction of windows where the pair was significant. This is the same window the EA re-runs live, so both stages of the system use the same definition.
Treat this num
ber as an activity indicator, not a calibrated statistic. It is affected by three factors:
The comparison uses raw p-values with no Benjamini-Hochberg step, so it is more permissive than the headline test. The windows are 1,500 bars long and step 250, so each window shares five sixths of its rows with the next one and the "fraction of significant windows" is an average over heavily dependent tests rather than independent ones. And the lags inside every window are the ones BIC picked on the training slice, which carries the selection problem from the previous section into every point on the curve. A stability of 43% means the relationship shows up in some stretches and not others. It does not mean there is a 43% chance the pair is real.
Finally, p-values across all four pairs are corrected with Benjamini-Hochberg:

"p_adj"

"p_value"

"fdr_bh"

1

"p_adj"

"stability"

"oos_edge_bps"

0

"status"

"p_value"

1e-8

"F-test mismatch with statsmodels"

The correction is there because we are testing four pairs at once. With four tests at 5%, the probability of at least one false positive is noticeably above 5% without it.
What it covers is exactly those four final tests and nothing else. The lag search, the rolling windows, the threshold we changed after seeing the results, and the separate tester optimizations later in the article are all additional looks at the same data, and none of them enter the correction. Counting only the pieces we can count, the four reported comparisons sit inside a much larger search, so BH here should be read as a minimum adjustment rather than a complete one.

Evaluation and Visualization
Once all four pairs have been tested, the results table is printed in a format that mir
rors the layout of the EA panel. The panel shows the live p-value once the EA has run its own test, so its numbers will differ from the notebook's adjusted values; it is the layout that carries over.
T
his makes it easy to compare the offline notebook verdict against what you later see on the chart.
The sum
mary and the two charts in this section were produced in the exploratory run, which is why M30 -> M15 shows as VALID and its bar is green. Under the pre-fixed STABILITY_MIN = 0.60 that status is INVALID and all four bars are red; the bar heights and the rolling curves do not depend on the threshold.

Step 9 produces the two charts used in the article. The left panel is a bar chart of significance per pair, expressed as negative log10 of the adjusted p-value so that taller bars mean stronger evidence. Bars above the dashed alpha line are significant. The right panel plots the rolling causality strength over time for all four pairs on the same axis, which shows not just whether a relationship exists but when it is active.
The bar color maps directly to status: green for VALID, red for INVALID. On EURUSD, M30 -> M15 is the only green bar. In the rolling chart, the orange M30 -> M15 line is the only one that rises above the dashed threshold with any regularity, and it does so in bursts rather than continuously. Neighbouring points on that curve are computed from windows that share most of their rows, so the line moves smoothly by construction and a burst is fewer independent events than it looks.

InpShowSignals only affects presentation: the signal line on the panel, the per-pair forecasts and the arrows on the chart. The signal is still computed, published and traded when it is off. Setting the signal timeframe below the lag timeframe of a pair does not add information, it only changes how often the same unchanged forecast is looked at. Keeping InpSignalTF equal to the smallest lag timeframe in the pair list is the setting the analysis actually supports.

MathCumulativeDistributionF in <Math\Stat\F.mqh> takes a tail flag whose meaning is easy to misread, and in the library source that flag is documented as the switch for the lower tail.
So tail = true returns P(F ≤ fStat), and passing true and then taking 1.0 - cdf would also give the right number. We pass tail = false instead,

If anything goes wrong in the calculation, the p-value defaults to 1.0, which makes the pair INVALID. Failing towards "no causality" is the safer direction for a filter.

The ridge term in FitOLS is a deliberate compromise. It keeps X'X invertible under near-collinearity. However, it also means the residuals and the resulting F-statistic are only approximate. The F-ratio built from those residuals is therefore an approximation of the classical statistic rather than the statistic itself. At 1e-9 relative to return variances measured in basis points the distortion is small, and you

for: Granger causality is a direct way to test whether the past values of series X improve the forecast of series Y beyond what Y's own past already provides — i.e., predictive content, not real-world causation
The test is implemented as an F-test comparing two nested OLS models: restricted (only lag-TF own lags) vs. unrestricted (plus lead-TF lags), with lags selected by BIC
A pair is marked VALID only if its Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-value < ALPHA (0.05) AND its rolling stability (fraction of significant 1,500-bar windows) ≥ STABILITY_MIN (pre-fixed 0.60)

The EA re-runs the same Granger F-test live on the most recent 1,500 bars using identical alignment logic, lag counts (p=1, q=2 for M30→M15), and window size — and uses the resulting forecast as a vote for signal generation
The final signal is generated by counting votes *only from pairs whose status is VALID* when the filter is on, making the rule both concrete and falsifiable

against: The trading signal uses a Granger causality test that requires alignment of higher-timeframe bars with lower-timeframe bars based on their open/close timing — but the live MQL5 implementation computes the forecast for the *current* (still-forming) lower-timeframe bar using data from higher-timeframe bars that have already closed *by the time the lower bar opens*. However, the signal decision (vote direction and magnitude) is applied to the *ongoing* bar — and the EA's logic (e.g., 'pred' used for voting, 'InpMinEdgeSigma' thresholding, and subsequent trade execution) treats that forecast as actionable *before the bar closes*. Since the forecast is of the bar’s return — which is only known after close — and the vote is used to generate signals *during* the bar (as confirmed by 'InpRetestBars' triggering every N lag-TF bars and 'InpShowSignals' drawing arrows on chart), the system implicitly relies on the forecast of an *unclosed bar*, i.e., future information (the final return) is not available at decision time. Crucially, the article states: 'The target variable y is [...] the log return of the current lag-timeframe bar', and 'What matters is the sign of the forecast, which becomes the vote direction'. But the vote is generated *before* that bar closes — so the forecast is used as if it were a deterministic proxy for the yet-unknown outcome. This violates causality: the signal depends on a model output whose ground truth (the bar’s actual return) is not available until bar close — yet the EA acts on it mid-bar. While not explicitly using future price values, the *trading logic treats the forecast as a real-time directional signal for the current bar*, which is functionally equivalent to acting on incomplete (future-dependent) information.

The rule cannot be written as a precise, unambiguous entry condition because the final signal is defined only as 'counting votes, but only from pairs whose status is VALID when the filter is on' — and 'status' is itself a dynamic, multi-layered, non-binary construct: it depends on (a) offline CSV verdict (which may be exploratory), (b) live retest p-value (raw, uncorrected), (c) InpStatusSource mode (OFFLINE/LIVE/BOTH), and (d) runtime validity filtering ('InpUseCausalityFilter'). Nowhere does the article specify *when exactly* a vote is cast, *how long it persists*, or *what price action triggers execution*: e.g., is a +1 vote acted upon on next tick? On bar open? On bar close? The EA code shows 'pred' and 'vote' are updated per retest, but no explicit entry logic (e.g., 'if vote == +1 and no position, then buy at market') is described in the article — only that 'the final signal comes from counting votes'. The inputs mention 'InpSignalTF' and 'InpCloseOnOpposite', but the article never defines the signal’s temporal binding: is it a bar-level signal (acted on at bar close) or tick-level? Without that, the rule is architecturally specified but operationally underspecified.

The Granger test fundamentally relies on the mechanical aggregation relationship between timeframes (e.g., 'An M30 log return is the sum of the two M15 log returns inside it'), and the article explicitly admits: 'Our design cannot separate [whether higher-TF carries new info vs. merely substitutes for omitted own lags]'. It further states: 'A fair test of "does an external driver push this market around" needs two different instruments, not two timeframes of one.' Thus, the core statistical premise — that Granger causality between M30 and M15 on EURUSD reflects predictive power of *independent information* — is invalidated by construction. The article concedes the test measures 'mechanical overlap', not true exogeneity. Therefore, the idea is built on a logically incoherent foundation: applying Granger causality to nested timeframes of the same symbol violates the independence assumption required for meaningful interpretation — making the entire causal gate concept theoretically unsound.
non_fatal: No out-of-sample validation of the final trading rule (backtest period 2023–2024 is *earlier* than calibration period 2026; thus, it tests backward generalization, not forward live use).

Lag selection via BIC on training data without correction for multiple testing inflates significance (acknowledged in text: 'Selecting lags and testing the selected model on the same data inflates significance').
Rolling stability metric uses overlapping windows (step=250, window=1500), violating independence assumptions — but this affects interpretation, not rule executability.
The EA uses ridge regression (small regularization) in FitOLS, making the live F-statistic an approximation — but the article treats it as equivalent to the offline OLS F-test.
The backtest is explicitly stated to be 'a demonstration that the pieces work together, not as evidence that the filter improves trading', indicating lack of performance validation.

judge.reject_reason: Фатальный порок: правило не может быть записано как чёткое детерминированное условие входа, поскольку статья не описывает конкретное, однозначное условие срабатывания сигнала (например, 'открыть лонг при условии X на цене Y в момент Z'). Вместо этого сигнал определяется как 'подсчёт голосов от валидных пар', но не указано: (1) когда именно голос фиксируется (на открытии бара? на тике? после расчёта прогноза?), (2) как голос преобразуется в конкретное решение входа (цена, тип ордера, момент исполнения), (3) как обрабатываются конфликты, срок действия голоса, временная привязка к бару. Кроме того, прогноз используется для оценки *текущего, ещё не закрывшегося* бара — что создаёт скрытую зависимость от будущего значения (фактического возврата бара), так как сигнал генерируется до его завершения, а целевая переменная y — это именно этот незавершённый возврат. Это нарушает причинность и делает невозможным построение корректного правила для спот-форекса без использования данных будущего.
judge.author_oos_metrics: Автор сообщает, что backtest проводился на периоде 2023–2024, который полностью предшествует периоду калибровки (апрель–сентябрь 2026), и подчёркивает, что это не симуляция live-торговли, а демонстрация совместной работы компонентов; out-of-sample edge для M30→M15 составил -0.035 bps, а OOS hit rate (50.0%) хуже базовой модели (51.9%).
judge.summary: Статья описывает методологию интеграции Granger-анализа для мультивременных фильтров в форекс-торговле, но не формулирует конкретное торговое правило с чётким условием входа. Основной фатальный порок — использование прогноза возврата *ещё не закрывшегося* бара в качестве основы для торгового сигнала, что технически эквивалентно использованию будущей информации, поскольку фактический возврат становится известен только после закрытия бара.
